opus-5.5.text:
Sure. I think this is one of the most under-examined assumptions in how we measure AI progress.

Look at almost any benchmark today, whether it's SWE-bench, a math benchmark, or some agent environment. You have, say, five hundred tasks. You run the model on each one independently, usually in parallel, and then you average the scores. Each task starts from a blank slate: the model has no memory of what it did on task one when it starts task two. Statistically that's very clean. It's i.i.d., it's reproducible, it's cheap to run. That's why everyone does it.

But think about how intelligence actually creates value in the real world. A human software engineer doesn't solve each GitHub issue as if it were the first day on the job. On day one in a new codebase you're slow, you read a lot, you make mistakes. By month three you know where everything is, you know the team's conventions, you know which tests are flaky. Your performance on task five hundred depends heavily on the previous four hundred ninety-nine. The value comes from that accumulation, from getting familiar with an environment over time.

Our evaluation setup explicitly throws that away. By resetting everything between tasks, we're measuring a kind of "day-one intelligence" over and over. And then we're a bit surprised that models crushing these benchmarks don't seem to change the economy as much as the numbers suggest. Part of the gap, I think, is exactly this: the benchmark rewards solving isolated puzzles, while the real world rewards systems that learn continuously, build memory, and adapt to a specific user, codebase, or organization.

There's also a deeper point about what the metric pushes research toward. Researchers optimize whatever the benchmark measures. If the benchmark is "average over independent runs," you get better and better one-shot problem solvers, bigger reasoning chains, more test-time compute per task. You don't get much pressure to solve long-term memory, online learning, or how an agent should organize its experience. Those problems stay under-researched not because they're unimportant, but because the scoreboard doesn't see them.

So when I say we should overturn this assumption, I don't mean i.i.d. evaluation is useless. It was the right tool for the first half of AI, when the main question was whether we could build models and methods that generalize at all. Now that we have very strong general priors from pretraining and reasoning from RL, the bottleneck shifts. The question becomes: can the system actually get better at your job the longer it does your job? To measure that, you need sequential evaluation, where tasks come in a stream, the agent keeps state, and you care about the trajectory of performance, not just the average.

That's harder to design. It's messier, less reproducible, and it raises questions about what counts as fair memory or leakage. But I think redefining evaluation like this is one of the most important things the field can do right now. In the second half of AI, deciding what to measure might matter more than how to train.

r001.rationale: The candidate contrasts benchmarks that average independent, reset task runs with a human engineer whose performance improves through accumulated experience in the same codebase.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the deepest issue is that the way we evaluate AI right now inherits a set of assumptions from the training setup, not from how intelligence actually gets used in the world.

Think about how a benchmark works today. You have, say, five hundred tasks. You run the model on each one independently, in parallel, with a clean context, and then you average the scores. Every task is i.i.d., every episode starts from zero. That's a very natural assumption if your mental model is supervised learning or classic RL on Atari, because that's literally how the data is structured. But it quietly bakes in a claim about what intelligence is, and I think that claim is wrong.

Because no human works like that. If you hire a software engineer, you don't give them five hundred independent tickets and reset their memory between each one. They do the first task, they learn something about the codebase, they make a mistake, they remember it, and the hundredth task they do is much better than the first. The whole point of a good employee is that they get better over time within the job. The evaluation we run on models completely erases that dimension. It can't even see it. A model that learns nothing from experience and a model that learns a lot look identical on an i.i.d. benchmark, as long as their first-attempt accuracy is the same.

So when I say the assumption needs to be overturned, I mean the unit of evaluation has to change. Instead of measuring average performance across parallel, independent runs, you should be measuring performance over a long, sequential stream of tasks, where the model is allowed to carry state, and you look at the curve. Does it improve? How fast? Does it stop repeating errors? That's the quantity that actually matters for a lot of real deployment.

And there's a second problem, which is that the i.i.d. setup makes the task artificially easy to specify. Every task comes with a clean reward and a clean reset. In the real world, reward is sparse, delayed, and often the environment is the one that gives you the feedback in a messy way. So the parallel-run paradigm also hides how much of the difficulty we've been removing from the problem.

I also think this is one of the reasons we're seeing a gap between benchmark numbers and perceived usefulness. The models are saturating a lot of these tests, and yet people still feel like the models don't "get" them, don't accumulate context, don't become a better collaborator over weeks. That gap is precisely the dimension our evaluation refused to measure. If you can't measure it, you don't optimize it, and then you shouldn't be surprised when it doesn't show up.

So my view is not that current benchmarks are useless. They were right for the phase we were in. But we're entering a phase where the interesting thing about an agent is what happens over time, with memory and interaction, and the evaluation has to be rebuilt around that. Otherwise we'll keep climbing the wrong hill.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts averaging independent benchmark runs with a human employee learning from earlier tasks and performing better over time.

astra-6.text:
I think that assumption makes sense if you’re evaluating a fixed model on a collection of independent questions. You run each question separately, average the scores, and ask, “How capable is this model?” But for an agent that learns through interaction, independence is a very strong restriction. It removes part of the capability we actually care about.

Imagine an agent working with you over a hundred tasks. On the first task, it doesn’t know your preferences or your tools. It makes mistakes, gets feedback, and hopefully learns something. By the hundredth task, it should be much better. If we evaluate those hundred tasks in parallel, with every run starting from the same initial state, we’re effectively measuring its first day at work a hundred times.

That can also change which system looks better. One agent might have stronger initial performance but repeat the same mistakes forever. Another might start slightly worse but improve quickly. An average over independent runs favors the first kind of capability and cannot really tell us about the second.

So I would question independence more than aggregation itself. We still need measurements, but we should also evaluate sequences of tasks where experience carries forward. Does feedback improve later decisions? Does the agent retain useful knowledge? Can it transfer a lesson to a different situation? And what does that improvement cost?

The shift is from asking only, “What can this system do right now?” to also asking, “What can this system learn by doing?” For a useful long-term agent, that second question is essential.

r001.rationale: The response explains why independent task runs miss an agent’s improvement with experience, and uses “first day at work” as an analogy. It does not clearly identify evaluating human workers by how much they improve over time.

sol-6.1.text:
I think that assumption makes sense when you’re evaluating a model as a static function: give it a thousand independent questions, average the scores, and see which model is better. But an agent operates over time. What it does now changes what it can do next, and ideally it learns from the experience.

Imagine an agent fails at a task, receives feedback, and then encounters a similar task tomorrow. If we reset it between every evaluation, we can measure its initial ability, but we can’t tell whether it improves or keeps making the same mistake. We’re removing the very thing we want to study.

The average can also hide problems that matter in practice. An agent might succeed on most isolated tasks but struggle to sustain progress through a long sequence, recover from an error, or recognize when it needs help. For a user working with that agent over weeks, those properties are crucial.

So I wouldn’t say we should abandon parallel evaluation. It’s useful and efficient. But it shouldn’t be our only model of evaluation. We also need to evaluate trajectories: how an agent uses feedback, accumulates useful knowledge, and becomes a better collaborator over time.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts independent task averages with measuring an agent’s learning over time, but it does not identify the comparison with how human workers are evaluated by improvement through experience.
